hints: Look at the melting and boiling points first, what type of structure must have values over 2000 degrees?
Focus on the conductivity pattern, poor as a solid but good as a liquid is the classic signature of one bonding type.
Both remaining ionic candidates fit the conductivity, so use solubility in water to pick the insoluble giant oxide.
walkthrough:
**Use the very high m.p. and b.p.**

Very high values like $2072^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $2980^{\circ}\text{C}$ tell you this is not a simple molecular substance.

It must have a giant lattice, either giant ionic, giant metallic or giant covalent, with many strong bonds to break.

**Use conductivity to find the bond type**

Remember the rule: metals conduct as solids, ionic compounds conduct only when molten or aqueous, covalent compounds do not conduct at all.

Here solid is poor but liquid is good, so mobile ions are released on melting. This points to giant ionic: $$\text{solid ionic (ions fixed) = poor, liquid ionic (ions mobile) = good}$$

**Use solubility to choose the exact substance**

Typical Group 1 ionic salts like sodium fluoride are soluble in water, but W is insoluble.

Aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, is a giant ionic lattice with high charge density and partial covalent character, so it has an extremely high m.p., conducts when molten, and is insoluble in water. That matches all the data perfectly.

options.A: Aluminium oxide, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, is a giant ionic lattice. Its high ionic charges give a very high m.p. and b.p., it cannot conduct as a solid because ions are fixed but conducts well as a liquid when ions are mobile, and its high lattice energy makes it insoluble in water.
options.B: Iron is a giant metallic lattice. Delocalised electrons would make it a good electrical conductor as a solid, not poor. Its m.p. around $1538^{\circ}\text{C}$ is also lower than the value given.
options.C: Silicon dioxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, is giant covalent with a very high m.p., but it has no mobile ions or electrons. It would be poor at conducting electricity both as a solid and as a liquid, not good as a liquid.
options.D: Sodium fluoride, $\text{NaF}$, is giant ionic and shows the poor solid, good liquid pattern, but it is soluble in water and has a much lower m.p. near $993^{\circ}\text{C}$. The insolubility and extremely high m.p. rule it out.
